transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:32 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Aidan Murphy (Cypress, Head of ML), Priya Kapoor (Cypress SRE), Liam Chen (CPO/CTO)

Summary (auto):
High-level discovery to understand Cypress's latency and throughput SLOs for an LLM recommendation/anti-fraud pipeline. Interested in differences between Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for p95 latency at scale, streaming behavior, and token/sec benchmarking. Action items: benchmark plan, share security docs, pricing.

Topics (auto):
- p95 latency targets and typical concurrency
- streaming vs non-streaming throughput
- tokens/sec benchmarks and batching behavior
- Dedicated capacity and VPC/network requirements
- SOC2 / KMS / data residency questions

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hi everyone thanks for joining, i'm jordan lee from redwood, i'm the account exec on this one, with maya our senior se. you folks good?
[00:09] Aidan: yep, thanks jordan. a quick intro: i'm aidan, head of ml at cypress. we run a real time recommender and some anti-fraud scoring. latency is... like, critical. p95 on user-facing flows needs to be around 120 to 200ms depending on path.
[00:24] Priya: hi all, priya here, i'm the s r e and i'll be validating network and infra constraints. we prefer VPC peering or private link, nothing that routes outbound to third party nets.
[00:36] Maya: great, thanks. can you give us a sense of concurrency and token patterns? are calls short prompts or long streaming sessions?
[00:44] Liam: most are short, 30-60 tokens for recs, but we have some batch scoring for fraud where it can be 1-2k tokens. concurrency spikes are the issue — during peak checkout we see 500-1k concurrent requests, sustained for 10-15 minutes.
[01:01] Jordan: ok so p95 <=200ms for user paths, that is tight. rough question: is that with streaming enabled or do you need the full response before rendering?
[01:10] Aidan: for recs we stream top results as they come, so streaming latency matters a lot — first-byte p50 ideally <50ms, p95 <150ms. for fraud batch jobs we can tolerate higher latencies.
[01:23] Maya: got it. two main levers: model choice/size and deployment mode. hosted has fastest onboarding but shared capacity and noisier tail; dedicated gives you reserved GPUs and more predictable p95, private gives full control for VPC/on-prem. we usually show token/sec and tokens per second benchmarks plus p95 numbers.
[01:41] Priya: also curious about batching and how kv cache works with streaming. sometimes KV is mis-labeled in our notes, like cache of prompts, but we mean key-value attention cache.
[01:52] Maya: yes KV cache for autoregressive models, that impacts repeated calls and context window performance. when streaming + kv cache, the runtime keeps the cache warm and you see better token/sec for subsequent calls.
[02:05] Jordan: to ground this, maya do you want to walk through the benchmark matrix we usually run?
[02:09] Maya: sure. typical matrix: single-request latency (cold vs warm), streaming first-byte latency, sustained throughput at various concurrencies, tokens/sec for different model sizes and quantization settings, and p95 at target concurrency. we also do tail noise analysis — 95/99 and long tail percentiles.
[02:27] Aidan: what kind of numbers do you see on hosted for p95 with smaller open models at, say, 64 concurrency?
[02:34] Maya: depends on model and hardware. for a 7B open model on P4/RTX-like hardware we might see median token latencies low but p95 can be 2-3x median under multi-tenant pressure. on dedicated you'd get much tighter p95 since you control scheduling and can pin capacity. typically hosted p95 at 64 concurrency maybe 200-400ms for short prompts but varies.
[02:52] Priya: that's... a wide band. can dedicated hit our p95 of 150ms consistently at 500 concurrent sessions?
[02:59] Maya: we design dedicated clusters to meet SLAs; for 500 concurrency streaming with short 30 token prompts, you need to size GPUs and batcher behavior. we often recommend autoscale pools plus burst capacity. rough calc: 500 concurrent * 30 tokens * (tokens/sec per GPU) — if a GPU can sustain 20k tok/s for that model, you'd be fine, but if it's lower you need more GPUs or quantized variants.
[03:20] Liam: tokens/sec per GPU... how do you measure that? is it end-to-end with network and serialization overhead?
[03:26] Maya: yes we measure end-to-end in our benchmark harness — includes serialization, routing, KV cache hit/miss, and TLS overhead. we produce tokens/sec, p50/p95 latency for first byte and full response.
[03:36] Jordan: we can share a benchmark sheet; we'll propose a run that mirrors your production traffic.
[03:40] Aidan: fantastic. also, what about streaming vs batching tradeoffs? sometimes batching helps throughput but increases first-byte latency.
[03:49] Maya: exactly. continuous batching improves GPU utilization and lowers cost per token, but adds queueing latency. for user-facing short prompts we keep batch windows tiny or bypass batching and rely on lower-latency execution kernels. for longer batch workloads (fraud scoring) we enable larger batching windows.
[04:04] Priya: do you support token-level cost/latency breakdowns? we need to attribute cost per route.
[04:09] Jordan: yes the console shows token-level cost and latency per route/model and per-request traces. helps optimizer decisions.
[04:16] Aidan: ok, operational constraints. we need SOC2, SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS for encryption. does hosted satisfy that?
[04:24] Jordan: Hosted is SOC2 compliant; we can integrate with your SAML SSO and provide audit logs. For KMS and BYOK, dedicated and private give stronger options: you can bring your key via HSM integrations on dedicated or the private control plane. we'll attach docs.
[04:37] Maya: also note data residency options on private deployments if you need region isolation.
[04:42] Liam: network egress: Priya wants to avoid public internet calls from our VPC. what's the path for private link?
[04:49] Maya: we support VPC peering, PrivateLink, and customer-managed VPNs depending on deployment. for hosted we typically provide PrivateLink so traffic stays within the cloud region. for private on-prem we deploy a control plane in the customer VPC.
[05:01] Priya: good. another question: what's the benchmarking cadence? we want to see p95 under synthetic load and also a replay of production traces.
[05:10] Maya: we do both — synthetic microbenchmarks to isolate tokens/sec and kernel performance, and full replay with representative prompts to measure end-to-end p95. we can run against our hosted test cluster or spin up a dedicated trial cluster in your account for more accurate results.
[05:26] Aidan: if we do dedicated trial in our account, how long to provision?
[05:29] Jordan: for a short proof we can provision a small dedicated pool in 2-4 days pending capacity. private deployments take longer (weeks) because of networking and security reviews.
[05:39] Liam: capacity planning question: if we want p95 <150ms streaming at 500 concurrency with 30 token responses, what would a back-of-envelope sizing look like?
[05:48] Maya: back-of-envelope: 500 concurrent * 30 tokens = 15k tokens in flight. If each GPU sustains 15k tok/s for that model, that's about 1 GPU to keep steady-state token/s, but streaming and latency headroom plus spikes means you'd want 3-4 GPUs plus autoscale buffer. We also consider kernel latencies — short prompt overhead matters. So we usually recommend measuring with your exact model and prompts.
[06:12] Priya: can you do a test run that simulates the checkout spike pattern (500-1k conc for 10 minutes)?
[06:17] Maya: yes, that's part of the benchmark plan. we'll define sustained and burst scenarios and measure p50/p95/p99.
[06:23] Jordan: i'll also include pricing for burst capacity and our SLA language.
[06:28] Aidan: what about quantization? can that help keep p95 down? any caveats for quality?
[06:33] Maya: quantization (4-bit/8-bit) can increase throughput and reduce memory; it usually helps latency on many kernels. tradeoff is potential small quality delta — we recommend evals on your prompt set. Redwood Optimize gives suggestions and automatically flags regressions with your evals.
[06:47] Liam: excellent. on the topic of evals, can you integrate our internal eval suite?
[06:51] Maya: yes we ingest prompt sets and can run automated regressions and quality monitoring tied to rollouts.
[06:57] Priya: security review — we'll want a SOC2 pack, network diagrams, any pen test reports.
[07:02] Jordan: we'll attach SOC2, architecture diagrams for private and dedicated, and a red-team summary.
[07:07] Aidan: good. one small point: earlier you said token/sec per GPU numbers like 20k — can you give a concrete example for a 7B quantized model vs a 13B quantized model?
[07:16] Maya: example numbers (very rough): 7B quant on A100-like perf might do 30-50k tok/s; 13B may do 12-20k tok/s depending on context length and kernel; larger models drop further. These are ballpark and depend on prompt complexity and kv cache hit rates.
[07:33] Aidan: ok we will share real traces so you can size accurately.
[07:38] Jordan: next steps recap: maya will draft benchmark plan, i'll send pricing + security docs, aidan will share traffic/profile, priya will validate network constraints and confirm PrivateLink preference. schedule follow-up for next week.
[07:50] Liam: sounds good. any blockers from our side?
[07:53] Priya: need to confirm who owns infra access for benchmarking. it'll likely be me.
[07:58] Maya: for the dedicated trial we need a service account and minimal IAM roles to spin up GPU instances; we can provide the exact list.
[08:07] Jordan: i'll follow up with a checklist in the email.
[08:11] Aidan: cool. quick aside — have you done streaming tests where first-byte is prioritized over throughput? some vendors let you configure preemptive scheduling for low-latency streams.
[08:21] Maya: yes, we support latency-priority scheduling policies for dedicated pools. you can enforce per-route priorities and fallback to cheaper models if latency degrades.
[08:31] Aidan: nice. also curious about observing tail jitter — do you expose per-token timing metrics?
[08:36] Maya: we provide per-token timing in trace hooks for evaluation runs and selective production sampling. console shows token-level histograms per API key/route.
[08:46] Liam: ok we have what we need. look forward to benchmark plan.
[08:50] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll send artifacts and pencil in follow-up.
[08:54] (call ends)
